query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-energy ball milling (mechanical alloying) step to W and Cu powders prior to spark-plasma sintering will produce a W–Cu composite with significantly reduced void fraction and improved interfacial contact, yielding higher thermal conductivity and mechanical durability under fusion-relevant irradiation compared to conventional infiltration of molten Cu into a W skeleton.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles and Cu powder, mixed in appropriate ratios for the desired composite.
generation.intervention: High-energy ball milling (mechanical alloying) of W and Cu powders prior to spark-plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Ball milling under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, followed by spark-plasma sintering at optimized temperature and pressure for W–Cu composites. Service conditions: thermal cycling and neutron irradiation as in fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial contact and reduced void fraction between W and Cu phases due to mechanical alloying, leading to a more uniform microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical alloying breaks up agglomerates, increases surface area and contact between W and Cu, and promotes diffusion during sintering, minimizing phase separation and void formation. This improves thermal transport and mechanical durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional Cu infiltration into W skeletons, the mechanically alloyed and SPS-sintered W–Cu composite will show at least a 20% increase in thermal conductivity and improved mechanical strength (e.g., flexural strength), with fewer voids and more uniform microstructure.
generation.baseline: W skeleton filled with molten Cu (conventional infiltration method).
generation.boundary: Processing: Ball milling and SPS must be performed under inert atmosphere; excessive milling time or temperature may cause contamination or unwanted phase formation. Service: Valid under fusion-reactor joint thermal cycling and irradiation; extreme neutron flux or temperature may degrade performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact increase in thermal conductivity and mechanical strength depends on milling parameters and sintering conditions; insufficient milling or improper sintering may not achieve the predicted improvements. Potential for contamination or unwanted phase formation exists.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one via conventional Cu infiltration into W skeleton, and one via high-energy ball milling of W and Cu powders followed by spark-plasma sintering. Subject both to thermal cycling and neutron irradiation. Compare microstructure, void fraction, thermal conductivity, and mechanical strength.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (laser flash or steady-state method)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically alloyed and SPS-sintered W–Cu composite does not show at least a 20% improvement in thermal conductivity or mechanical strength, or if void fraction and interfacial contact are not improved relative to the conventional baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
